About the Genetics event

Genetics is a Health Professions event in the HOSA secondary division. Format: testing · skills.

Ten in-depth lessons for HOSA’s new Genetics event, following the 2026–27 test plan and every Round Two skill: DNA extraction, bacterial conjugation and transduction, Drosophila and Wisconsin Fast Plants crosses, cross interpretation and the chi-square test. Includes Punnett square, chi-square, DNA-to-protein, Hardy-Weinberg, gel and transformation labs. The official reference is Carolina’s guidebook for the HOSA Genetics test; always follow the scenario and rating sheets you are given.

Genetics lessons

Unit 1 · Cell division and reproduction

Test plan: reproduction, mitosis and meiosis 20%.

  1. The Genetics event, the cell cycle and mitosis 30 min

    Every one of the trillions of cells in your body came from a single fertilized egg, copied with remarkable accuracy. Genetics begins with how cells copy their DNA and divide—and it is the first piece of the 20%…

  2. Meiosis and sexual reproduction 30 min

    Two siblings with the same parents can look very different. Meiosis is the reason: it halves the chromosome number and shuffles genes so that each egg and sperm is genetically unique. Understanding meiosis explains…

Unit 2 · Classical and chromosomal inheritance

Test plan: classical genetics 20%, chromosomal inheritance 10%. Skill IV.

  1. Mendelian genetics and Punnett squares 35 min

    In a monastery garden in the 1850s and 1860s, Gregor Mendel crossed thousands of pea plants and counted their offspring. His ratios—3:1 and 9:3:3:1—revealed that traits are passed on as discrete units we now call genes…

  2. Beyond Mendel: non-Mendelian inheritance and pedigrees 30 min

    Pink snapdragons from red and white parents, AB blood type and skin color with many shades all break Mendel’s simple dominant–recessive pattern. Skill IV asks you to recognize these patterns, solve a blood-typing cross…

  3. Chromosomal inheritance, sex linkage and linkage maps 30 min

    In 1910, Thomas Hunt Morgan found a single white-eyed male fruit fly among red-eyed siblings. Tracking that trait showed for the first time that a specific gene sits on a specific chromosome—the X. Chromosomal…

Unit 3 · Molecular genetics and the laboratory

Test plan: molecular genetics 15%, experimental design and model organisms 15%. Skills I and II.

  1. Molecular genetics: DNA, RNA and protein 30 min

    A single change in one DNA base—an A replaced by a T—changes one amino acid in hemoglobin and causes sickle cell disease. Molecular genetics (15% of the test) explains how DNA stores information, copies itself and…

  2. Experimental design, model organisms and DNA extraction (Skill I) 35 min

    Why study fruit flies to understand human disease? Because flies, bacteria, yeast and fast-growing plants share genes and processes with us and reproduce quickly. Experimental design and model organisms make up 15% of…

  3. Bacterial genetics, gene transfer and biotechnology tools (Skill II) 30 min

    Bacteria reproduce asexually, yet they swap genes constantly—which is how antibiotic resistance can spread through a hospital. Skill II has competitors move genes between E. coli strains by conjugation or with a virus…

Unit 4 · Crosses, statistics, populations and careers

Test plan: population genetics 10%, modern applications and careers 10%. Skills III and V.

  1. Test crosses with Drosophila and Fast Plants; chi-square (Skills III and V) 30 min

    Mendel counted peas; you will sort sleeping fruit flies and pollinate tiny flowers with a wand. Then you will ask whether your counts fit the expected ratio—or whether the difference is too large to be chance. Skills…

  2. Population genetics, modern applications and careers 30 min

    If 1 in 2,500 newborns has a recessive condition, about 1 in 25 people carries the allele without knowing it. Population genetics (10%) explains how allele frequencies behave and change, and modern applications and…

Sample Genetics questions

1. An organism with a dominant phenotype is crossed with a homozygous recessive organism to find its genotype. What is this called?

  1. A back cross with the dominant parent
  2. A test cross
  3. A dihybrid cross
  4. A reciprocal cross
Show answer

B. A test cross

If any offspring show the recessive trait, the unknown parent must be heterozygous.

2. Which statistical test compares observed offspring counts with the counts expected from Mendelian ratios?

  1. Chi-square test
  2. t-test only
  3. Correlation coefficient
  4. Standard deviation
Show answer

A. Chi-square test

The chi-square test shows whether differences between observed and expected results are likely due to chance.

3. A female with a single X chromosome (45,X) has which condition?

  1. Klinefelter syndrome
  2. Down syndrome
  3. Edwards syndrome
  4. Turner syndrome
Show answer

D. Turner syndrome

Turner syndrome can cause short stature and ovarian failure. Klinefelter syndrome is 47,XXY in males.
